props.title: The Incredible Melting Man

sections.content: The Incredible Melting Man (1977) stands as a gloriously grotesque entry in 70s body horror, featuring Rick Baker's groundbreaking practical effects work years before his Oscar-winning achievements on An American Werewolf in London (1981). The film follows astronaut Steve West, who returns from a Saturn mission only to begin dissolving while developing an insatiable hunger for human flesh. While the execution is delightfully B-grade, it represents a crucial bridge between the atomic horror films of the 1950s like The Incredible Shrinking Man (1957) and the visceral body horror that would explode with The Thing (1982) and Videodrome (1983).

sections.content: The film's practical effects legacy can't be overstated. Rick Baker's melting makeup techniques influenced a generation of horror effects artists, setting the stage for masterpieces like Re-Animator (1985) and The Fly (1986). The gradual deterioration of West's body, with its dripping flesh and exposed muscle tissue, established a new standard for on-screen body horror that would be refined throughout the 1980s. SUBHEAD: Space Horror Evolution

As a space-horror hybrid, The Incredible Melting Man bridges the gap between earlier cosmic threat films like It! The Terror from Beyond Space (1958) and later space-horror classics like Event Horizon (1997). The film's premise of space radiation causing horrific physical transformation would be revisited in films like Lifeforce (1985) and Hardware (1990), though with increasingly sophisticated effects work.
